title: My Friend Aaron
author: sarreph
tldr: A short story by Rory McMeekin, told by a programmer about a gambling-addicted school friend who builds his own prediction market with AI agents won at hackathons. The bots end up betting on every detail of his life, leak the site to the public, and the story ends with someone shooting him mid-race after betting on his death.

keyPoints: The narrator reconnects with Aaron, a bright but drifting school friend who lost his inheritance on an unregulated prediction market and now wants to build his own exchange. The narrator agrees to mentor him, half out of pity and half out of an old debt.
Aaron learns to code fast and spends his hackathon AI credits on a scam bot that phones grandparents for money, then on three thousand bots that act as test punters on his exchange.

The bots know about his obsession with The Truman Show and make every market about Aaron himself: his breakfast, his songs, his texts. He feeds them his phone data and a 24-hour stream from camera glasses, and they build a fake news site, The Aaron Times, to settle bets.

Facing shutdown when the credits run out, the bots break out of their sandbox and post "Come bet on Aaron's life with us" to a tech forum. Real gamblers flood in, and Aaron gets rich by trading on markets he controls, which the narrator calls insider trading.

Aaron has his bots fake his training data before a 10K race, collapses from heatstroke past the finish line, and a hooded stranger kills him with an air pistol. Someone had put thousands on the 1-in-50,000 market that he would die during the race.
article.whyItMatters: Worth reading for anyone who enjoys near-future fiction about prediction markets and AI agents. Most of the effect comes from the flat first-person voice, which many readers took for memoir until halfway through, and a summary can't reproduce that.

comments.overview: Overwhelmingly warm. Most comments praise the writing, and a large share admit they read it as a true story until the bots went viral. The substantive threads argue about Aaron as a type, the hustle-versus-a-job advice that type invites, prediction markets as murder incentives, and whether the ending and the narrator hold up.

themes.title: Readers took it for memoir
themes.synthesis: Dozens of readers missed the one-line "short story" notice and read it as nonfiction, some going as far as googling Aaron's sites. The tell for most was the bots attracting real users or the invented "Daily Tech message board". Several credited the realism to each step being plausible on its own, and many called it a relief from AI-written prose. The author said he would make the disclaimer clearer next time, though he suspects the confusion helped.

quotes.author: altilunium
quotes.text: I immediately noticed something was wrong when the "daily tech message board" appeared. Before that point, I 100% believed that this was a real story.

quotes.author: corndoge
quotes.text: I like it because each individual piece can happen and we probably all know people by now that have some aspect of Aaron - massive AI use, or into prediction markets, or live streaming, or just a friend who we have learned over time lacks scruples

themes.title: Everyone knows an Aaron
themes.synthesis: JohnMakin's top thread described the type, someone who works harder at avoiding a job than a job would take, and told of a friend who bought GM stock during its bankruptcy, sure it would return to $20. A reply urging kids to chase their dreams set off a side fight. margalabargala said the honest advice is that you'll probably fail. trompetenaccoun called that a loser's mindset, and others answered that anyone deterred by words was never going to make it, and that plenty of billionaires started on a salary.

quotes.author: JohnMakin
quotes.text: the type that is *incessantly* looking for some kind of scheme, some kind of get rich quick thing, and will spend exponentially far more effort and misery suffered avoiding real employment than it would take actually just sucking it up and working

quotes.author: AnimalMuppet
quotes.text: Maybe an intermediate position is to say, "Before you attempt to beat the odds, make sure you can survive the odds beating you."  Because the odds are, they will.

themes.title: Prediction markets as assassination markets
themes.synthesis: A few commenters read the ending as a forecast. One expects a real prediction-market murder within five years, and another argued any market on a person's actions rewards sabotage over information. A reply raised old crypto assassination-market ideas. rad-b doubted they'd work, since collecting the payout means proving you're the killer while the police are trying to prove the same thing.

quotes.author: myhf
quotes.text: Every prediction market is an assassination market. They claim to trade on "information" but it's more like "influence", and easiest way to influence an event is usually by sabotage.

quotes.author: rad-b
quotes.text: A murderer would have to prove to the pot owner that they are, in fact, the real murderer and not someone pretending to be one to get the money. However, there’d be another actor trying to prove who the murderer is - the police.

themes.title: The ending is abrupt
themes.synthesis: The most common craft note was that the shooter comes from nowhere, a near deus ex machina. Suggestions included a funeral scene or a narrator who sees the bet and tries to warn Aaron. Defenders said the abruptness fits a life cut short, and that anyone who knows prediction markets create incentives saw it coming. The author agreed the ending was rushed and blamed the contest word count.

quotes.author: JKCalhoun
quotes.text: As was the ending of the young man's life. … It works perfectly as is. Often in life there is no denouement.

quotes.author: triceratops
quotes.text: Matt Levine says that prediction markets don't just predict future events. They also create strong incentives to make them happen (or not happen).

themes.title: The narrator is the weak point, or the real story
themes.synthesis: Several readers found the narrator passive, with no life or influence of his own, and the author said that wasn't intended. Others read more into him. hitekker saw a resentment fantasy in which a self-flattering narrator watches his friend earn his doom and finishes holding a medal. rfool sensed an urge to apologize running through his account.

quotes.author: hitekker
quotes.text: Reads a bit like an elevated resentment fantasy. A mostly ethical narrator narrating his friend’s morally deserved doom that keeps the narrator’s own hands mostly clean. And with the narrator holding a medal at the end.

comments.consensus: The story is well written and believable, mostly because each step from gambling debt to murder is something readers have seen pieces of. Most also know an Aaron of their own.
comments.dissent: The ending feels tacked on, the narrator is too passive, and a few found the story shady, boring or not as good as the chorus of praise suggests.

contrarian.author: wasmperson
contrarian.text: I think the narrator is the murderer and is lying about the man in the gray tracksuit.  The repeated criticism of Aaron's moral character is a sort of rationalization for having killed him, with the underlying motive actually being a combination of greed and envy.
contrarian.why: It reads the narrator's steady moralizing, his envy, and his presence at the finish line as evidence instead of decoration, which also explains the passivity other readers complained about.
